title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with meat and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of egg white prepared as an omelet, scrambled eggs, or fried, combined with lean meat (such as chicken, turkey, or lean beef) and a variety of vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper, onion). It provides high‑quality protein, vitamins and minerals, while being low in fat and carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is almost pure protein and contains virtually no fat or carbs.
Cooking egg white without the yolk reduces the cholesterol content of the meal.
Pairing protein with vegetables increases the bioavailability of certain nutrients, e.g., vitamin C from tomatoes enhances iron absorption from meat.
Quick cooking methods (scrambling or frying) preserve heat‑sensitive vitamins such as vitamin B6.
The dish can be prepared in a microwave or skillet in 5‑10 minutes, making it popular among people with busy lifestyles.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Egg white and meat supply a complete set of essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Absence of yolk and use of lean meat keep the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal provides riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Meat and vegetables deliver iron, zinc, magnesium and potassium, supporting electrolyte balance.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from vegetables and antioxidant properties of egg white help strengthen immune defenses.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using processed meat or sauces can raise sodium levels; opt for fresh, unsalted meat and season lightly.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive browning can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Large servings may lead to excess calories, especially if the dish is prepared with added oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whisk the egg white, add diced lean meat and chopped vegetables. In a lightly oiled hot skillet, cook as an omelet, scramble, or fry, stirring until the egg white is fully set. Season with salt, pepper and herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The prepared dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave to retain texture.
